entries.name: scaling hypothesis
entries.senseHere: The bet that simply making neural networks bigger, with more data and computing power, will eventually produce general intelligence. The strong version says no new ideas are needed; the weak version says new algorithms are still needed, just run at huge scale.

entries.name: GPT-3
entries.background: A very large language model released by OpenAI in 2020, with 175 billion adjustable numbers (parameters). It was trained to predict the next word of Internet text.

entries.name: meta-learning
entries.senseHere: A model picking up a new task from a few examples or instructions in its prompt, without being retrained. GPT-3 was never built to do this.

entries.name: GPT-2
entries.background: OpenAI's 2019 language model with 1.5 billion parameters. It could write fluent text and was the direct predecessor of GPT-3.

entries.name: OpenAI
entries.background: An AI research lab founded in 2015 that built the GPT models. It later created a for-profit arm to raise money for large-scale training.

entries.name: blessings of scale
entries.senseHere: The observation that in deep learning, bigger systems often get easier to train and better at generalizing. Problems that plague small networks vanish as size grows.

entries.name: unsupervised learning
entries.background: Learning from data with no human-written labels or answers. A language model learns from raw text by predicting what comes next.

entries.name: Transformer
entries.background: A neural network design from 2017 that uses a mechanism called self-attention to relate every part of the input to every other. It underlies GPT models.

entries.name: scaling laws
entries.background: Regular mathematical patterns showing that model error falls smoothly and predictably as model size, data and computing power rise.

entries.name: AGI
entries.background: Artificial general intelligence: AI that can handle a broad range of intellectual tasks at roughly human level, rather than one narrow task.

entries.name: Hans Moravec
entries.background: Robotics researcher who in the 1990s forecast that human-level computing power would become affordable in the 2020s. He argued AI progress would follow falling hardware costs.

entries.name: reinforcement learning
entries.background: Training a system by rewarding good actions, as when a game-playing program learns from wins and losses.

entries.name: Jukebox
entries.background: An OpenAI model released in 2020 that generates raw music audio, including singing voices.

entries.name: pretraining thesis
entries.senseHere: The argument that training a model only to predict the next piece of text forces it to learn logic, causality and understanding. Predicting well at the very end requires real comprehension.

entries.name: Turing-NLG
entries.background: A 17-billion-parameter language model from Microsoft, the largest before GPT-3.

entries.name: AlphaGo Zero
entries.background: DeepMind systems that learned games like Go, chess and StarCraft (AlphaStar) mostly by playing themselves. MuZero learned without even being told the rules.

entries.name: loss
entries.background: A number measuring how badly a model predicts. For text it is the average bits of surprise per character, and lower is better.

entries.name: Bitter Lesson
entries.background: Richard Sutton's 2019 essay arguing that AI progress has mostly come from more computing power rather than clever hand-designed methods.

entries.name: neural nets are lazy
entries.senseHere: Networks grab the easiest shortcuts, like memorizing or surface patterns, and only learn deeper skills when data and tasks are hard and varied enough to make shortcuts fail.

entries.name: DeepMind
entries.background: A London AI lab owned by Google. It built AlphaGo, AlphaZero and AlphaStar, game-playing systems that reached superhuman skill.

entries.name: agency
entries.senseHere: The ability to pursue goals by planning actions. The author treats it as a matter of degree rather than a yes-or-no property, so a model trained on human text can pick it up.

entries.name: double descent
entries.background: A puzzling pattern where bigger models first get worse at new data, then get better again as they grow past a certain size.

entries.name: lottery ticket hypothesis
entries.background: The idea that a big network contains many small sub-networks, and some happen to be able to learn the task well on their own.

entries.name: hardware overhang
entries.senseHere: A situation where computers powerful enough for a breakthrough already exist, but nobody has yet spent the money or effort to use them that way.

entries.name: Ilya Sutskever
entries.background: Co-founder and chief scientist of OpenAI, long a believer that large neural networks plus data and compute would work.

entries.name: intentional stance
entries.background: Philosopher Daniel Dennett's idea of explaining a system by treating it as if it had goals and beliefs. It works even for non-human things like thermostats.

entries.name: variational principle
entries.background: The physics idea that a system's behavior can be described as it choosing the path that minimizes or maximizes some quantity, like light taking the fastest route.

entries.name: SayCan
entries.background: A Google robotics system that uses a language model to turn spoken instructions, such as fetching a drink, into steps a real robot carries out.

entries.name: Janus
entries.background: Online pseudonymous writer on language models who views GPT as a simulator of the world rather than as an agent.

entries.name: Conway's Game of Life
entries.background: A grid game where cells live or die by simple neighbor rules, producing moving shapes like gliders. It is a famous example of complex behavior from simple rules.

entries.name: Turing machine
entries.background: Alan Turing's abstract model of a computer: a head reading and writing symbols on a tape following fixed rules. Any computation can be done on one.

entries.name: Occam's razor
entries.background: The principle that the simplest explanation fitting the facts is usually best.
